query: The Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms several primary non-eutectic phases during solidification and exhibits a complex, multistep crystallization sequence. Under rapid cooling, slower cooling, and subsequent reheating assessed by thermal analysis, what single intervention could increase amorphous retention and thermal stability while overcoming extensive primary crystallization? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the alloy’s reported glass formation and crystallization behavior, the relevant cooling-rate and reheating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-applying an ultrathin (~5 nm) Al2O3 passivation layer on the mold or melt container interfaces prior to melt spinning will significantly increase amorphous retention and thermal stability in the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy by reducing heterogeneous nucleation, thereby delaying crystallization onset during controlled reheating.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy prepared in thin-plate or ribbon form via melt spinning.
generation.intervention: Deposit a ~5 nm Al2O3 coating on the inner surfaces of the casting mold or melt container prior to processing, followed by rapid melt spinning (cooling rates >10^6 K/s) and subsequent controlled reheating (10–20 K/min) through the DSC crystallization regime.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed in an argon atmosphere. The Al2O3 coating is applied using established thin-film deposition methods and verified with in situ characterization to ensure its stability during rapid quenching. Rapid cooling is performed via melt spinning, ensuring cooling rates in excess of 10^6 K/s, with a controlled reheating regime to probe crystallization behavior in the DSC temperature window.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction of heterogeneous nucleation sites at the interface due to the inert, passivating Al2O3 layer.
generation.mechanism: The pre-applied Al2O3 layer acts as a chemical and physical barrier that minimizes contact between the molten alloy and substrate impurities or oxide particulates, thus lowering the number of sites available for heterogeneous nucleation. This barrier inhibits early nucleation of primary crystalline phases during rapid solidification and delays crystallization during reheating. In situ monitoring ensures that the coating sustains integrity during processing.
generation.predicted_outcome: The passivation intervention is predicted to yield a higher retained amorphous fraction and an increase in the onset temperature for crystallization compared to uncoated samples. The alloy should display suppressed primary crystallization even under varied cooling rate and reheating conditions.
generation.baseline: Standard processing without the oxide passivation normally results in multiple non-eutectic primary crystalline phases and a lower thermal stability (earlier crystallization onset) during reheating.
generation.boundary: Cooling rates: >10^6 K/s as in melt spinning; Reheating rates: controlled ramp of 10–20 K/min up to the crystallization temperature range (approximately 600–650°C). The approach is applicable to thin-plate/ribbon samples.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about whether the passivation layer fully prevents nucleation from impurities beyond the mold interface and how uniform the coating remains under extreme thermal gradients, which will necessitate thorough in situ characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy samples: one processed with the pre-applied ultrathin Al2O3 coating and one without. Apply identical melt spinning (cooling rate >10^6 K/s) and controlled reheating (10–20 K/min) protocols. Use in situ high-speed imaging and synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction or TEM to verify the integrity of the passivation layer during solidification and, subsequently, monitor the onset of crystallization during reheating.
measurements: Assessment of amorphous volume fraction via XRD and TEM
Determination of crystallization onset temperature using DSC
In situ evaluation of coating integrity during rapid quenching (via high-speed imaging or time-resolved spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in amorphous retention or a delay in the crystallization onset temperature compared to the non-passivated controls, or if in situ monitoring reveals rapid degradation of the Al2O3 layer during processing, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Samples, including CoCrNi, CoCrFeNi, and CoCrFeMnNi, were prepared by traditional casting, LDED, and LPBF, respectively. The as-cast samples with the same composition were prepared by arc-melting constituent elements with 99.99% purity under an argon atmosphere. The cast ingot was flipped and remelted multiple times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The annealed CoCrNi sample was sealed in a quartz tube with argon and then heat-treated at 900 °C for 7 days. LDED was conducted using an Optomec Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS) 450 system with an IPG fiber laser (400 W) at a wavelength of 1064 nm and a laser spot size of ~400 μm at the focal point. During the printing process, the chamber was filled with high-purity argon as an inert gas to keep the oxygen level below 20 ppm. The LDED typically relies on feeding powders into the melt path and molten pool created by a laser beam to deposit material layer-by-layer upon a substrate part or build plate. The LPBF samples were prepared using a commercial M290 (EOS) LPBF machine with a maximum power of 400 W and a focal diameter of 100 μm. All samples were prepared in an argon environment with an oxygen concentration of less than 1000 ppm.

This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. The cooling rates were systematically varied, with slow cooling averaging approximately 52 K/s, accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning achieving rapid cooling rates in the range of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s. The role of phosphorus in promoting phase stability and modifying solidification pathways is further supported by phase diagram analysis. Binary [] and ternary [] phase diagrams indicate that phosphorus addition promotes the formation of phosphide phases, which appear as independent intermediate phases or within eutectic systems. Moreover, phosphorus significantly reduces the solidification temperature range of primary, phosphorus-poor phases. Cooling profiles recorded during solidification, both after remelting on a copper plate and following a brief electric arc pulse, suggest the presence of low-phosphorus phases, such as phase “A”, and phosphide-rich phases, including those forming in eutectic (“B” + “D”) or non-eutectic systems (“C” and “E”). The obtained results indicate that phosphorus plays a significant role in shaping the crystallization process and the resulting microstructure; however, its influence should be considered in the context of interactions with other elements present in the complex multicomponent system.

The cooling profile recorded during welding (at a cooling rate of 154 K/s) demonstrates that the Cantor alloy solidifies at a temperature of 1478 K []. Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. proposals.intervention: Apply a high‐intensity pulsed electromagnetic field (PEMF) during solidification
proposals.conditions: Perform melt spinning or suction casting with cooling rates in the range of 10^5–10^6 K/s while imposing a pulsed electromagnetic field (field strengths on the order of 1–5 Tesla, pulse durations of microseconds) during the rapid quench; subsequent reheating is done with a controlled ramp (e.g., 10 K/min) up to the conventional crystallization onset temperature (around 600–650°C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Disruption of incipient crystalline nuclei formation by modifying the atomic diffusion and local ordering during solidification
proposals.mechanism: The imposed electromagnetic pulses interact with the magnetic elements (e.g., Mn, Fe, Co) to induce spin disorder and transient magnetic forces that impede atomic mobility and diffusion pathways, thus raising the nucleation barrier for primary crystallization. This delays or suppresses the formation of non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification, and possibly during reheating as well
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under PEMF-assisted rapid quenching, the alloy is predicted to retain a larger amorphous fraction and exhibit improved thermal stability (i.e., a higher crystallization onset temperature and reduced extent of primary crystalline phases) compared with the baseline behavior, as the disruptive field lowers the probability of primary crystal nucleation even at slower cooling and reheating conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This intervention targets the critical need to suppress primary non-eutectic crystallization during both rapid cooling and slower cooling/reheating sequences by interfering directly with the nucleation kinetics. It provides a single processing modification that can improve glass forming ability and thermal stability

proposals.intervention: Implement high-pressure melt quenching during solidification
proposals.conditions: Process the molten alloy under an applied hydrostatic pressure of 2–3 GPa during quenching with cooling rates around 10^5 K/s; subsequent reheating is performed at ambient pressure using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at controlled heating rates (e.g., 10 K/min) up to the crystallization regime
proposals.structural_mediator: Pressure-induced modification of the thermodynamic free energy landscape that increases the nucleation barrier for crystallization
proposals.mechanism: The applied pressure reduces the atomic mobility and alters the free energy difference between the liquid and crystalline phases. This increased barrier to nucleation effectively suppresses the formation of primary crystalline phases during cooling and delays the onset of crystallization during reheating
proposals.predicted_outcome: The high-pressure intervention is expected to yield an alloy with enhanced amorphous retention and a shift of the crystallization onset to higher temperatures compared to conventional quenching under ambient pressure. This leads to improved thermal stability and reduced extensive primary crystallization
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By using high pressure as a single processing intervention, the approach directly addresses the challenge of excessive primary crystallization, ensuring a more stable amorphous structure over a broader range of cooling rates and during subsequent thermal treatments

proposals.intervention: Introduce an ultrathin surface oxide passivation layer prior to melt quenching
proposals.conditions: Deposit a ~5 nm Al2O3 coating on the inner surfaces of the casting mold or on the melt container prior to processing; then perform high cooling rate techniques such as melt spinning with rates in excess of 10^6 K/s, followed by controlled reheating (e.g., 10–20 K/min) up to the DSC crystallization region
proposals.structural_mediator: Reduction of heterogeneous nucleation sites at the melt container interface due to the inert and passivating nature of the coating
proposals.mechanism: The pre-applied Al2O3 layer acts as a chemical and physical barrier that minimizes contact between the molten alloy and substrate impurities or oxide particles that normally serve as nucleation sites. This inhibition of heterogeneous nucleation results in the retention of a higher fraction of the amorphous phase during solidification and delays subsequent crystallization upon reheating
proposals.predicted_outcome: The intervention is predicted to substantially increase the amorphous volume fraction and enhance the thermal stability (i.e., raising the onset temperature for crystallization) compared with standard processing without passivation; the alloy would exhibit reduced primary crystallization even under moderate cooling rates and reheating conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single processing intervention directly tackles the severe primary crystallization issue by eliminating extrinsic nucleation triggers, thereby offering a viable path to improved glass formation and thermal stability throughout various cooling and reheating regimes

proposals.material_system: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, processed as thin surface layers
proposals.intervention: Utilize laser-induced surface remelting with rapid quenching
proposals.conditions: Apply a high-intensity nanosecond pulsed laser (energy density tuned to fully melt a superficial ~50 µm layer) to locally remelt the as-cast alloy, achieving cooling rates on the order of 10^6 K/s. Follow this with controlled lower-power laser annealing for reheating within the 600–650°C range at defined intervals
proposals.structural_mediator: Creation of a highly homogeneous, fine-scale structure by eliminating preexisting heterogeneous nucleation centers via a localized remelting and ultra-rapid solidification process
proposals.mechanism: The laser remelting fully resets the microstructure at the surface and the ultra-rapid quenching that follows prevents the formation of crystalline nuclei. The subsequent, precisely controlled laser annealing enables subtle relaxation without triggering widespread crystallization, thus fostering thermal stability
proposals.predicted_outcome: This intervention is predicted to yield a surface layer with significantly higher amorphous retention and an elevated crystallization onset temperature compared to conventionally cooled samples, effectively suppressing the complex multistep crystallization sequence associated with primary phases
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: Laser-induced surface remelting is a single, localized intervention that effectively overcomes extensive primary crystallization by homogenizing the microstructure and preventing the formation of nucleation sites; this controlled approach bridges the conflicting cooling-rate and reheating conditions by providing a tailored thermal history to maximize glass formation and thermal stability

critiques.addresses_problem: Yes – reducing heterogeneous nucleation by passivating the melt–container interface directly targets the crystallization triggers causing extensive primary phase growth.
critiques.constraints: Yes – it respects the constraints by working with the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 system in thin-plate/ribbon form and is tailored to the high cooling rate (≥10^6 K/s) and controlled reheating conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically plausible; an ultrathin Al2O3 layer can act as a barrier to impurity-induced nucleation, reducing extra nucleation sites.
critiques.feasibility: Deposition of a 5 nm Al2O3 coating is an established technique and integrating it with melt spinning is practical.
critiques.evidence: There is supportive literature on interfacial passivation reducing heterogeneous nucleation in similar systems, although no specific record IDs are provided here.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the coating may not fully inhibit nucleation from sources other than the substrate interface (e.g., from within the melt or container-derived contaminants) or might degrade during processing.
critiques.fix: Perform in situ characterization of the coating’s stability during melt quenching and validate its effect on nucleation sites beyond the interface.

decision.rationale: Direction A is chosen because it directly targets the suppression of heterogeneous nucleation by passivating the melt–container interface, thereby reducing the initiation sites for primary crystallization. The critic's suggested fix—conducting in situ characterization to ensure coating integrity during rapid processing—is reasonable and addresses the main risk. This approach is feasible with established deposition techniques and aligns well with the cooling rates and reheating conditions relevant to the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy in thin-plate/ribbon form.
